title: CLARA: Clarification of Language Ambiguity through Result Analysis for Natural-Language Cancer Genomics Queries
comment: Preprint of an article submitted for consideration in the Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing (PSB 2027). Copyright 2026 World Scientific Publishing Company. https://psb.stanford.edu/
summary: A natural language interface can be used to make cancer genomics databases easier to use, but even if a question is perfectly fluent, its scientific meaning can be ambiguous. We propose CLARA, a framework that represents a question as a typed scientific query specification, considers a few possible interpretations, executes them, and asks for clarification when the estimates diverge. CLARA was assessed on mutation-prevalence contrasts among eight TCGA PanCancer Atlas cohorts and a 30-gene panel. This benchmark consisted of 330 unique executable contrasts varying in mutation scope, assay denominator, and sample context; 115 contrasts were result-sensitive and 215 were result-stable, per the preregistered definition of relative divergence greater than 0.10 or absolute divergence greater than 5 percentage points. An independently implemented pandas execution engine perfectly replicated all 660 results from the SQLite engine. In a separate 120-question LLM-generated, manually vetted language stress test, CLARA recognized all 60 result-sensitive contrasts and needlessly clarified 13 of 60 stable contrasts (accuracy 89.2%, sensitivity/recall 100%, specificity 78.3%). Standalone machine learning had superior overall accuracy (97.5%) but missed one critical contrast. This demonstrates that downstream execution can distinguish consequential from inconsequential ambiguity and reveal an explicit trade-off between safety and burden.

AI.tldr: CLARA is a framework for natural language interfaces to cancer genomics databases that represents questions as typed scientific queries, explores multiple interpretations, executes them, and asks for clarification only when results diverge. It distinguishes consequential from inconsequential ambiguity via downstream execution, achieving 89.2% accuracy on a language stress test while catching all critical contrasts.
AI.motivation: Natural language interfaces to cancer genomics databases are hard to build because even fluent questions can be scientifically ambiguous. The key insight is that ambiguity matters only when it changes the answer, so the framework should focus on result-sensitive ambiguity rather than all ambiguity.
AI.method: CLARA represents questions as typed scientific query specifications, generates a few possible interpretations, executes all of them, and asks the user for clarification only when the estimates from different interpretations diverge beyond a threshold (relative divergence > 0.10 or absolute divergence > 5 percentage points).
AI.result: On 330 unique executable contrasts across TCGA PanCancer Atlas cohorts, an independent pandas engine perfectly replicated all 660 results from SQLite. In a 120-question LLM-generated stress test, CLARA recognized all 60 result-sensitive contrasts, needlessly clarified 13 of 60 stable contrasts (89.2% accuracy, 100% sensitivity, 78.3% specificity). Standalone ML had higher overall accuracy (97.5%) but missed one critical contrast.
AI.conclusion: Downstream execution of multiple interpretations can effectively separate consequential from inconsequential ambiguity in scientific questions, revealing an explicit trade-off between safety (catching critical contrasts) and user burden (unnecessary clarifications).

title: Frozen but Not Always Accessible: A Representation Analysis of Genomic Language Models
summary: Genomic foundation models are increasingly reused as frozen feature extractors for downstream sequence prediction, offering a compute-efficient alternative to full fine-tuning. However, it remains unclear when biological information encoded by these models is accessible without task-specific adaptation. We present a representation-accessibility analysis of frozen genomic language models across regulatory, epigenetic, promoter, splice-site, and variant-effect prediction tasks. We evaluate DNABERT-2, Nucleotide Transformer, HyenaDNA, GENERATOR-v2, and Omni-DNA under unified frozen-probing protocols, while separating diagnostic readout analyses from validation-selected checks. Our results reveal a consistent task-dependent pattern: frozen probes recover 95-100 % of fine-tuned performance on promoter tasks, but average splice-site recovery drops to 60-88 %. Frozen embeddings are also competitive on broad Genomic Benchmark tasks such as coding-region and species-discrimination classification, but show larger gaps on some regulatory and OCR tasks. Layer-wise probing, in-silico mutagenesis, variant-effect prediction, and embedding geometry show that local biological signal is partially present in frozen representations, but is not always accessible through final pooled embeddings.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes whether frozen genomic foundation models can access biological information without task-specific fine-tuning, finding that frozen probes recover 95-100% of fine-tuned performance on promoter tasks but only 60-88% on splice-site tasks, with layer-wise analysis revealing that local biological signals are partially present but not always accessible through final pooled embeddings.
AI.motivation: To determine when biological information encoded in frozen genomic language models is accessible without task-specific adaptation, since these models are increasingly reused as frozen feature extractors for downstream sequence prediction as a compute-efficient alternative to full fine-tuning.
AI.method: Conducts a representation-accessibility analysis of five frozen genomic language models (DNABERT-2, Nucleotide Transformer, HyenaDNA, GENERATOR-v2, and Omni-DNA) across regulatory, epigenetic, promoter, splice-site, and variant-effect prediction tasks using unified frozen-probing protocols, separating diagnostic readout analyses from validation-selected checks. Includes layer-wise probing, in-silico mutagenesis, variant-effect prediction, and embedding geometry analyses.
AI.result: Frozen probes recover 95-100% of fine-tuned performance on promoter tasks but average splice-site recovery drops to 60-88%. Frozen embeddings are competitive on broad Genomic Benchmark tasks like coding-region and species-discrimination classification, but show larger gaps on some regulatory and OCR tasks.
AI.conclusion: Local biological signal is partially present in frozen representations but is not always accessible through final pooled embeddings, revealing a task-dependent pattern of representation accessibility in genomic foundation models.

title: IL-10 rs1800896 polymorphism predicts biochemical remission in IBD patients undergoing biologic therapy
comment: 22 pages; 2 main tables and 1 main figure; supplementary tables and figure included. Pre-peer-reviewed author manuscript. The final article was published in Immunology, 2026, volume 177, issue 2, pages 432-438
summary: Background. Genetic factors, including single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), may modulate disease course and therapeutic efficacy in patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Aim. We investigated the association between four SNPs in cytokine genes and clinical phenotype as well as the response to molecular-targeted drugs in patients with IBD. Materials and Methods. A total of 197 IBD patients (142 Crohn's disease [CD], 55 ulcerative colitis [UC]) undergoing targeted treatment were enrolled. The SNPs analyzed were TNF-alpha rs1800629 (-308 G>A), TGF-beta rs1800471 (codon 10 C>T), IL-6 rs1800795 (-174 G>C), and IL-10 rs1800896 (-1082 G>A). Biochemical response at 12 months (T12) was defined as CRP <5.0 mg/L and fecal calprotectin <250 microg/g at T12, in the absence of ongoing corticosteroid therapy. Results. The IL-6 rs1800795 C allele was significantly associated with a younger age at diagnosis (p=0.049), while the TNF-alpha rs1800629 A allele was more frequently observed in patients with CD than UC (p=0.036). Among 134 patients included in the per-protocol analysis, 41.0% achieved biochemical remission at T12. The IL-10 rs1800896 variant allele was associated with remission (OR 2.15, 95% CI 1.03-4.44; p=0.041), and the association remained significant in multivariable analysis (adjusted OR 4.15, 95% CI 1.49-11.56; p=0.007). Conclusions. Genotyping of cytokine-related SNPs may help identify patients with distinct disease phenotypes and support personalized treatment strategies in IBD.

AI.tldr: This study investigated the association between four cytokine gene SNPs (TNF-alpha, TGF-beta, IL-6, IL-10) and clinical phenotype plus treatment response in 197 IBD patients receiving molecular-targeted therapy. The IL-6 rs1800795 C allele was linked to younger diagnosis age, TNF-alpha rs1800629 A allele was more common in CD than UC, and the IL-10 rs1800896 variant allele was significantly associated with biochemical remission at 12 months (adjusted OR 4.15).
AI.motivation: To explore whether genetic factors (SNPs in cytokine genes) can predict disease course and therapeutic efficacy in IBD patients, which could enable more personalized treatment strategies.
AI.method: A total of 197 IBD patients (142 CD, 55 UC) undergoing targeted treatment were genotyped for four SNPs: TNF-alpha rs1800629, TGF-beta rs1800471, IL-6 rs1800795, and IL-10 rs1800896. Biochemical response at 12 months was defined as CRP <5.0 mg/L and fecal calprotectin <250 microg/g without ongoing corticosteroid therapy. Associations were assessed via univariate and multivariable analyses.
AI.result: IL-6 rs1800795 C allele correlated with younger age at diagnosis (p=0.049). TNF-alpha rs1800629 A allele was more frequent in CD than UC (p=0.036). Of 134 patients in per-protocol analysis, 41.0% achieved biochemical remission. IL-10 rs1800896 variant allele was associated with remission (OR 2.15, p=0.041), remaining significant in multivariable analysis (adjusted OR 4.15, p=0.007).
AI.conclusion: Cytokine-related SNP genotyping may help identify IBD patients with distinct phenotypes and support personalized therapeutic decision-making.

title: The ethics of artificial intelligence in the life sciences: Universality, cultural diversity and an architecture of care
summary: The life sciences and health research have started to benefit from artificial intelligence, which raises ethical concerns that are real but, we argue, not special. Any science should be governed by values that rest on how the human brain is built and socialised rather than anything distinct to artificial intelligence. Importantly, the human brain has a different, much less costly computational architecture than these machines. This is achieved through the orchestration of a global neuronal workspace, and through reward best described not as a quantity to be maximised but as a continuous cycle of wanting, liking and satiety. As such, this creates the deep tension running through the ethics of the human person, between the universality of ethical judgement and the diversity of morals. The brain networks of the global workspace and emotion are universally shared, but the diversity of content is shaped by epigenetic appropriation of the particulars of the physical, social and cultural world, which makes every person unique. Still, if we were to build machines on these principles rather than the present unaffordable reward maximisers, the question of their governance would change from restraint to upbringing. We set out the institutions such a future would require, together with the questions that remain open.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that AI ethics concerns are not unique to AI but grounded in human brain architecture and socialization. It proposes that building machines based on the brain's global neuronal workspace and reward-as-cycle (wanting, liking, satiety) principles would shift AI governance from restraint to upbringing, and outlines the institutional implications.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to reframe the ethical debate around AI in life sciences and health research, arguing that current concerns are not special to AI but fundamentally rooted in human neurobiology and social development. They challenge existing approaches and propose a new conceptual framework.
AI.method: The paper presents a conceptual/argumentative analysis drawing on neuroscience, specifically contrasting the human brain's computationally efficient architecture (global neuronal workspace, reward cycles) with artificial machine architectures (reward maximizers). It argues for a paradigm shift from governing AI through restraint to governing through upbringing, based on brain-inspired principles.
AI.result: The authors conclude that the tension between universal ethical judgment and moral diversity is inherent to human brain networks that are universally shared yet shaped by epigenetic and cultural influences. They propose a future where machines built on these principles would require a different governance model—one based on upbringing rather than restraint—and outline the institutions needed for such a future.
AI.conclusion: AI ethics should be understood through human neurobiology rather than as a distinct problem. The future of machine governance may shift from restrictive regulation to an upbringing-based approach, though significant open questions remain regarding implementation.

title: Effective pruning of task-trained recurrent neural networks using noisy fluctuations and connection rescaling
summary: The pruning of network connections is key to brain function but, despite its importance, there exist few biologically-plausible pruning rules with demonstrated good performance. In this work we evaluate noise-prune, a recently introduced unsupervised local pruning rule for recurrent networks that uses noisy fluctuations to determine the importance of connections. Noise-prune has previously only been empirically tested on random networks without a specific computational function. We show that noise-prune preserves task-performance in task-trained recurrent neural networks, greatly outperforming a strategy that only uses the magnitude of connections and performing on par with or exceeding a non-local strategy that uses second-order information. Rather than deterministically removing connections that fall below a certain threshold importance, noise-prune samples connections to preserve based on their importance and strengthens retained connections to preserve average synaptic strength. We show that this sampling and rescaling is essential to good performance, but that the optimal empirical degree of rescaling is lower than that predicted by the original theoretical argument. Our work thus validates noise-prune as a biologically-plausible pruning rule for functional recurrent network architectures and characterizes its optimal parameter settings.

AI.tldr: This paper validates noise-prune, an unsupervised local pruning rule for recurrent neural networks, showing it preserves task performance in task-trained networks, outperforms magnitude-based pruning, and matches or exceeds non-local second-order methods. The authors also characterize the optimal rescaling parameters, finding the empirical optimum is lower than theoretical predictions.
AI.motivation: Network pruning is crucial for brain function, yet few biologically-plausible pruning rules have demonstrated good performance. Noise-prune had only been tested on random networks without specific computational functions, leaving its applicability to functional recurrent networks unclear.
AI.method: The authors evaluate noise-prune, an unsupervised local pruning rule that uses noisy fluctuations to determine connection importance, on task-trained recurrent neural networks. They compare it against magnitude-based pruning and non-local second-order information strategies. They analyze the effect of sampling-based connection preservation and synaptic strength rescaling, and compare empirical optimal rescaling with theoretical predictions.
AI.result: Noise-prune preserves task performance in task-trained RNNs, greatly outperforming magnitude-based pruning and performing on par with or exceeding non-local second-order methods. Sampling and rescaling are shown to be essential for good performance, though the optimal empirical degree of rescaling is lower than originally predicted theoretically.
AI.conclusion: Noise-prune is validated as a biologically-plausible pruning rule for functional recurrent network architectures, and its optimal parameter settings are characterized.

title: From Local Learning to Global Prediction Through Layered Surprise Cascades
summary: Hierarchical predictive coding proposes a compelling hypothesis of brain computation, suggesting that the cortex builds layered predictions to minimize surprise. Yet most models rely on error-coding neurons or generative modeling of unclear biological plausibility. Here, we examine a biologically plausible framework in which the functional goals of predictive coding emerge from local contrastive learning and simple activity cancellation. Building on recent machine learning advances, we present a recurrent variant of the Forward-Forward (FF) algorithm with an inverted objective that increases activity for negative data. This setup yields predictive representations across layers, capturing hallmark features of cortical computation such as top-down modulation and surprise signaling. Our results suggest that key principles of predictive coding can emerge from simple, local learning rules, offering a new bridge between neuroscience and machine learning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a biologically plausible framework where predictive coding emerges from local contrastive learning via a recurrent variant of the Forward-Forward algorithm with an inverted objective.
AI.motivation: Existing predictive coding models rely on error-coding neurons or generative modeling that lack clear biological plausibility, motivating a simpler local learning framework.
AI.method: The authors present a recurrent variant of the Forward-Forward (FF) algorithm with an inverted objective that increases activity for negative data, enabling predictive representations to emerge across layers.
AI.result: The framework captures hallmark features of cortical computation, including top-down modulation and surprise signaling.
AI.conclusion: Key principles of predictive coding can emerge from simple, local learning rules, providing a bridge between neuroscience and machine learning.

title: Transcutaneous Spinal Cord Stimulation Disrupts Conscious Ankle Proprioception and Produces a More Constrained Locomotor Pattern in Unimpaired Adults
summary: Transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) modulates spinal sensorimotor circuits primarily through activation of afferent networks. While prior work has emphasized locomotor performance and spinal excitability, how tSCS affects conscious proprioceptive perception and the extent to which such effects parallel changes in locomotor control remain unclear. We investigated the acute and training-related effects of tSCS on ankle proprioception and gait in unimpaired adults (n = 14), with an independent control group (n = 14) completing identical proprioceptive training without stimulation. Proprioception was quantified using a bilateral robotic assessment of dynamic ankle localization ability (Crisscross), gross motor output using maximum dorsiflexion strength, and gait during normal and tandem treadmill walking using spatiotemporal, trunk-sway, and mediolateral center-of-mass (CoM) excursion measures. Acute tSCS increased ankle proprioceptive error (p < 0.001) while dorsiflexion strength was unchanged (p = 0.30). Gait shifted toward a modestly more constrained locomotor pattern, characterized by reduced step width and ML CoM excursion (p < 0.05). With continued training under stimulation, proprioceptive error decreased and, unlike the control group, the tSCS group showed progressive improvement that persisted after stimulation ended. Sagittal-plane gait measures recovered toward or beyond baseline, whereas mediolateral measures remained constrained, revealing a direction-dependent reorganization of locomotor control. Together, these findings show that tSCS influences multiple aspects of the sensorimotor control loop, disrupting conscious proprioception while reshaping locomotor behavior, and that the nervous system can adapt to altered afferent input through training.

AI.tldr: This study investigates how transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) affects conscious ankle proprioception and gait in unimpaired adults. Acute tSCS impairs proprioceptive accuracy while modestly constraining gait (reduced step width and center-of-mass excursion). With training under stimulation, proprioception progressively improved and persisted after stimulation ended, while gait showed direction-dependent reorganization—sagittal-plane measures recovered but mediolateral measures remained constrained.
AI.motivation: Previous research on tSCS has focused on locomotor performance and spinal excitability, but it remains unclear how tSCS affects conscious proprioceptive perception and whether such effects parallel changes in locomotor control. Understanding this gap is important for characterizing the full sensorimotor impact of tSCS.
AI.method: Fourteen unimpaired adults received tSCS with acute and training assessments, and an independent control group (n=14) performed identical proprioceptive training without stimulation. Proprioception was measured using a bilateral robotic dynamic ankle localization task (Crisscross), gross motor output via maximum dorsiflexion strength, and gait during normal and tandem treadmill walking using spatiotemporal, trunk-sway, and mediolateral center-of-mass excursion measures.
AI.result: Acute tSCS increased ankle proprioceptive error (p<0.001) without changing dorsiflexion strength (p=0.30). Gait became modestly more constrained with reduced step width and ML CoM excursion (p<0.05). With continued training under stimulation, proprioceptive error decreased and, unlike controls, the tSCS group showed progressive improvement persisting after stimulation ended. Sagittal-plane gait measures recovered toward or beyond baseline, while mediolateral measures remained constrained.
AI.conclusion: tSCS modulates multiple aspects of the sensorimotor control loop—disrupting conscious proprioception while reshaping locomotor behavior—and the nervous system can adapt to altered afferent input through training. These findings reveal direction-dependent reorganization of locomotor control under tSCS.

title: A Low-Power Wearable Respiratory Sensor for Non-Invasive Stress Monitoring
comment: Code available at this URL: https://github.com/mohamad-hoseini/FSResp
summary: Respiration provides a continuously available window into physiological state and behavior. However, monitoring it outside controlled settings remains challenging because a wearable system must capture small body deformations while remaining comfortable, low power, and robust to changes in posture and motion. We present a compact non-invasive respiratory sensing system based on a force-sensitive resistor (FSR) embedded in an abdominal belt and integrated with a custom Bluetooth Low Energy acquisition board. The system combines a simple piezoresistive readout with a mechanical holder designed to transfer abdominal expansion to the sensor without analog amplification. We evaluate the complete sensing pipeline across multiple breathing patterns and body positions. In stationary settings, the recorded signals exhibit consistent amplitude changes and recurring peak-to-peak timing across breathing maneuvers; under light movement, these variations remain visible despite motion-induced baseline shifts. We further design a five-phase stress-induction protocol and collect respiratory recordings from 12 participants. Using interpretable time-domain features and standard classifiers, we examine whether the acquired signals distinguish relaxation from stress-induction phases. In this preliminary experiment, the best-performing model achieves 88.0% test accuracy, indicating that the extracted respiratory features distinguish stress-induced phases from relaxation phases in this dataset. Overall, our results show that the proposed platform enables real-time respiratory monitoring across diverse daily-life scenarios and captures respiratory changes that distinguish stress-induction from relaxation phases, supporting its potential for affective-computing applications.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a compact, non-invasive respiratory sensing system using a force-sensitive resistor embedded in an abdominal belt with a custom BLE acquisition board. Evaluated across breathing patterns and body positions, and validated in a stress-induction study with 12 participants where the best classifier achieved 88.0% test accuracy in distinguishing stress from relaxation phases.
AI.motivation: Respiratory monitoring outside controlled settings is challenging because wearable systems must capture small body deformations while remaining comfortable, low power, and robust to posture changes and motion artifacts.
AI.method: The system uses an FSR embedded in an abdominal belt, integrated with a custom Bluetooth Low Energy acquisition board, a simple piezoresistive readout, and a mechanical holder that transfers abdominal expansion to the sensor without analog amplification. Evaluation includes a five-phase stress-induction protocol with 12 participants, using interpretable time-domain features and standard classifiers.
AI.result: Stationary signals show consistent amplitude and peak-to-peak timing across breathing maneuvers; variations remain visible under light movement despite baseline shifts. The best-performing model achieves 88.0% test accuracy in distinguishing stress-induced phases from relaxation phases.
AI.conclusion: The proposed platform enables real-time respiratory monitoring across diverse daily-life scenarios and captures respiratory changes that distinguish stress-induction from relaxation phases, supporting its potential for affective-computing applications.

title: Curriculum Multiple Shooting for Robust Training of Neural and Universal Differential Equations
summary: Neural ordinary differential equations (NODEs) and universal differential equations (UDEs) provide flexible and popular frameworks for learning interpretable dynamical systems from noisy time-series data. However, training these models remains challenging, and versatile methods that robustly handle sparse and noisy data as well as partially observed models are lacking. To address this, we introduce curriculum multiple shooting (CMS), a general-purpose training strategy for fitting ordinary differential equation (ODE) models to time-series data by integrating curriculum learning with multiple shooting. Across twelve benchmarks spanning simulated and real data, and covering NODEs, UDEs, and mechanistic ODEs, CMS accelerates and stabilises training convergence, outperforms state-of-the-art training strategies, and ranks among the best methods in generalisation. Finally, we discuss possible explanations for the strong performance of CMS in light of contemporary theories of what makes training on time-series challenging.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces curriculum multiple shooting (CMS), a general-purpose training strategy for fitting ODE models to time-series data by combining curriculum learning with multiple shooting. CMS accelerates and stabilizes training convergence across twelve benchmarks covering NODEs, UDEs, and mechanistic ODEs, outperforming state-of-the-art training strategies.
AI.motivation: Training NODEs and UDEs remains challenging, and existing methods lack versatility in handling sparse, noisy, and partially observed data. The authors aim to address this gap with a robust general-purpose training strategy.
AI.method: CMS integrates curriculum learning with multiple shooting—a training strategy that progressively increases data complexity while using multiple shooting to stabilize optimization over the time-series domain.
AI.result: Across twelve benchmarks covering simulated and real data, CMS accelerates and stabilizes training convergence, outperforms state-of-the-art training strategies, and ranks among the best methods in generalization.
AI.conclusion: CMS provides a robust and effective training approach for ODE-based models, and the paper discusses theoretical explanations for its strong performance in light of contemporary theories of time-series training challenges.

title: Complexity and Stability of Neural Activity Across Aging and Neurodegenerative Disease
summary: Objective: EEG signals fluctuate continuously even within a fixed cognitive state, but an important question is whether the brain still reuses similar activity patterns to represent information over time. Methods: To address this, we model EEG as distributions of windowed activity patterns and quantify their temporal stability using Wasserstein distance, while intrinsic dimensionality captures representational complexity. Results: Across multi-task, lifespan, and clinical EEG datasets, we find that neural representations show constrained, condition-specific stability rather than unconstrained drift. Higher intrinsic dimensionality is consistently associated with lower stability, suggesting that richer representational spaces are less reproducible over time. Both measures exhibit reproducible spatial organization, with posterior regions showing higher dimensionality and lower stability than frontal regions. Healthy aging is characterized by increased dimensionality and reduced stability, whereas mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease show a joint collapse of both. Conclusions: These findings provide a distribution-level framework for understanding neural stability across cognition, aging, and disease. Significance: This framework offers a principled approach to quantifying neural representational stability, with potential utility as a sensitive biomarker for tracking cognitive aging and neurodegeneration in clinical settings.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a distribution-level framework using Wasserstein distance and intrinsic dimensionality to quantify the temporal stability and representational complexity of EEG activity patterns, revealing constrained condition-specific stability, a consistent negative relationship between dimensionality and stability, and distinct signatures across healthy aging (increased dimensionality, reduced stability) versus neurodegeneration (joint collapse of both).
AI.motivation: The authors aim to address whether the brain reuses similar activity patterns to represent information over time, despite EEG signals fluctuating continuously even within a fixed cognitive state. They seek a principled way to quantify neural representational stability over time.
AI.method: EEG signals are modeled as distributions of windowed activity patterns. Temporal stability is quantified using Wasserstein distance between these distributions, while intrinsic dimensionality is used to capture representational complexity. The approach is applied across multi-task, lifespan, and clinical EEG datasets.
AI.result: Neural representations exhibit constrained, condition-specific stability rather than unconstrained drift. Higher intrinsic dimensionality consistently correlates with lower stability. Both measures show reproducible spatial organization (posterior regions: higher dimensionality/lower stability; frontal regions: the reverse). Healthy aging shows increased dimensionality and reduced stability, while mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease show a joint collapse of both measures.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a distribution-level framework for understanding neural stability across cognition, aging, and disease, offering a principled approach to quantifying neural representational stability with potential utility as a sensitive biomarker for tracking cognitive aging and neurodegeneration in clinical settings.

title: Convergent Evolution in Algorithmic Space
summary: In evolutionary biology, unrelated organisms can independently evolve similar structures when exposed to similar functional demands. Here we ask whether an analogous form of convergent evolution occurs during neural network training: do networks with different random initializations develop similar internal weight structures when trained on the same task? This question is technically nontrivial because hidden neurons can be arbitrarily permuted without changing the represented function, making direct matrix comparisons misleading. We introduce a matching-based framework for comparing multilayer perceptrons in structural weight space. Hidden neurons are first coarsely aligned using permutation-invariant features and then refined by iterative Hungarian matching. After alignment, networks are compared with structural distance metrics designed to emphasize task-relevant weight patterns. Applying this approach to ensembles of small MLPs trained on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and KMNIST, we find that networks trained on the same task remain closer to one another than to networks trained on different tasks. Thus, task-specific training appears to guide initially random networks toward distinct regions, or attractors, in structural network space. The earliest phase of training reveals an additional and unexpected phenomenon. Classification accuracy rises rapidly before the matched structural distances show strong task-specific separation, and before the global weight distribution visibly changes. Nevertheless, individual weight entries already begin to drift in a coordinated manner. This suggests that early learning may first operate through subtle, distributed adjustments that strongly affect function while leaving coarse network morphology almost unchanged. We treat this early morphogenesis as a first glimpse of a richer dynamical process that will be investigated in future work.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether neural networks with different random initializations converge to similar internal weight structures when trained on the same task, analogous to convergent evolution in biology. The authors introduce a matching-based framework for comparing MLPs in structural weight space, using permutation-invariant features for coarse alignment followed by iterative Hungarian matching, then apply structural distance metrics. They find that networks trained on the same task are closer to each other than to networks trained on different tasks, suggesting task-specific training guides networks toward distinct attractors in structural space. They also observe an early training phase where accuracy rises before structural separation appears, implying learning initially proceeds through subtle, distributed weight adjustments.
AI.motivation: The authors ask whether convergent evolution has an analog in neural network training—specifically, whether independently initialized networks trained on the same task develop similar internal weight structures. This is nontrivial because hidden neurons can be permuted without changing the function, making naive matrix comparisons meaningless.
AI.method: A matching-based framework for comparing MLPs in structural weight space. Hidden neurons are first coarsely aligned using permutation-invariant features, then refined via iterative Hungarian matching. After alignment, structural distance metrics emphasizing task-relevant weight patterns are used to compare networks.
AI.result: Networks trained on the same task (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, KMNIST) remain closer to one another than to networks trained on different tasks, indicating task-specific attractors in structural network space. Additionally, early training shows rapid accuracy gains before strong task-specific structural separation or global weight distribution changes occur, yet individual weights still drift in a coordinated manner.
AI.conclusion: Task-specific training guides initially random networks toward distinct regions (attractors) in structural weight space, analogous to convergent evolution. Early learning appears to operate through subtle, distributed adjustments that strongly affect function while leaving coarse network morphology nearly unchanged, offering a glimpse of a richer dynamical process for future investigation.

title: Convergent Evolution in Neural Representation Space: Emergent Order in Deep Belief Networks
summary: Deep Belief Networks (DBNs) learn hierarchical generative models without class supervision. Here, we ask whether this purely unsupervised process nevertheless organizes internal representations according to the unknown data classes. We analyze successive layers of DBNs trained on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and KMNIST using the Generalized Discrimination Value (GDV), supervised probes applied only after training, a reconstruction-based measure of abstraction distance, effective dimensionality, and free sample generation. Remarkably, class-specific clustering generally increases with depth across datasets and network widths, although no label information is available during DBN training. Control experiments show that this effect depends on the learned feature structure and cannot be explained by random transformations, weight marginals, dimensionality reduction, or sigmoid saturation. The first hidden layers also frequently make class identity more accessible to linear and nonlinear probes. With greater depth, representations become increasingly compact and prototype-like as neurons acquire correlated feature directions. At the same time, GDV and probe accuracy reveal complementary aspects of class structure: improved average clustering can coexist with reduced accessibility for a few difficult class pairs. These findings demonstrate that layer-wise generative learning can spontaneously uncover and progressively amplify class-related structure in unlabeled data.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether Deep Belief Networks (DBNs), despite being trained purely unsupervised, spontaneously organize internal representations according to unknown data classes. Using multiple analysis methods (GDV, supervised probes, reconstruction-based abstraction distance, effective dimensionality, and free sample generation) on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and KMNIST, they find that class-specific clustering generally increases with network depth, and that deeper layers produce increasingly compact, prototype-like representations. Control experiments rule out trivial explanations, demonstrating that layer-wise generative learning can progressively amplify class-related structure without any label supervision.
AI.motivation: The core question is whether unsupervised hierarchical generative models like DBNs, which learn without any label information, nonetheless organize their internal representations according to unknown class structure. This addresses whether class-related organization emerges purely from generative learning dynamics rather than explicit supervision.
AI.method: The authors train DBNs on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and KMNIST, then analyze successive layers using multiple complementary metrics: Generalized Discrimination Value (GDV) for clustering quality, supervised probes (linear and nonlinear) applied only post-training, a reconstruction-based measure of abstraction distance, effective dimensionality, and free sample generation. Control experiments test against random transformations, weight marginals, dimensionality reduction, and sigmoid saturation to isolate the effect of learned feature structure.
AI.result: Class-specific clustering generally increases with depth across datasets and network widths despite no label supervision. Control experiments confirm the effect depends on learned feature structure. First hidden layers make class identity more accessible to probes. Deeper layers yield compact, prototype-like representations with correlated feature directions. GDV and probe accuracy reveal complementary aspects—improved average clustering can coexist with reduced accessibility for difficult class pairs.
AI.conclusion: Layer-wise generative learning can spontaneously uncover and progressively amplify class-related structure in unlabeled data, suggesting that unsupervised representation learning inherently captures class-discriminative information as a byproduct of hierarchical generative modeling.

title: Simple evolution drives direct reciprocity to maximum payoff in social dilemmas
summary: Direct reciprocity is a mechanism for evolution of cooperation based on repeated interactions between the same individuals. Direct reciprocity can help natural selection to favor cooperators over defectors, but whether or not cooperation prevails depends on the details of the evolutionary dynamics. We describe simple processes of evolution that have the astonishing ability of driving direct reciprocity to maximum payoff in all social dilemmas which we study. The basic process is based on mutation and pairwise comparison. Mutation samples strategies near the boundary of the strategy space. Pairwise comparison includes a parameter for intensity of selection. For large population sizes, intermediate to high mutation rates and intermediate to strong intensities of selection, we find that the process leads to communities of strategies that reach maximum payoff in Prisoner's Dilemma, Snowdrift, Stag Hunt and Harmony games. Maximum payoff in all four games is consistently achieved if players have access to memory-2 strategies. Memory-1 strategies have the capacity to resolve all four social dilemmas, but they are usually defeated by a ``Hold-trap'' in Snowdrift games.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that a simple evolutionary process based on mutation and pairwise comparison can drive direct reciprocity to maximum payoff across all four social dilemmas (Prisoner's Dilemma, Snowdrift, Stag Hunt, and Harmony games), provided players have access to memory-2 strategies. Memory-1 strategies can resolve all dilemmas but typically fail in Snowdrift games due to a "Hold-trap."
AI.motivation: Direct reciprocity can favor cooperation over defection, but whether cooperation prevails depends on the details of evolutionary dynamics. The authors seek to identify simple evolutionary processes that robustly drive strategies toward maximum payoff across all social dilemmas.
AI.method: The evolutionary process combines two mechanisms: (1) mutation that samples strategies near the boundary of the strategy space, and (2) pairwise comparison dynamics with a parameter controlling the intensity of selection. The authors analyze this process for large population sizes, intermediate-to-high mutation rates, and intermediate-to-strong selection intensities, studying memory-1 and memory-2 strategies.
AI.result: The process drives communities of strategies to maximum payoff in all four games (Prisoner's Dilemma, Snowdrift, Stag Hunt, Harmony) when memory-2 strategies are available. Memory-1 strategies can resolve all four dilemmas but are usually defeated by a "Hold-trap" in Snowdrift games.
AI.conclusion: Simple evolutionary processes based on mutation and pairwise comparison can robustly achieve maximum payoff in all social dilemmas when sufficient memory (memory-2) is available to players, revealing that the architecture of strategy memory and evolutionary dynamics jointly determine the success of direct reciprocity.

title: Errorless Irrationality: A unified computational account of the inverse base-rate effect across predictive, observational, and unsupervised procedures
summary: The inverse base-rate effect is a robust bias in how people resolve ambiguity between competing categories, and the most prominent theories explain it through prediction error. Across two experiments we progressively removed the elements of the predictive-learning design that supply such error signals: first by moving to observational learning, then to an unsupervised procedure in which category labels were not presented. The effect persisted--the irrational bias is independent of supervised learning procedures. We propose a new theory, OSCAR, that integrates core computational principles of the best-validated models and operates on self-generated feedback akin to pattern completion. OSCAR extends the learning dynamics underlying the response bias to observational and unsupervised procedures. Evaluated on a large preexisting supervised dataset in addition to the two new experiments reported here, OSCAR performs competitively against alternatives, and is the first model that reproduces the pattern of individual differences seen in humans across all three procedures. The model provides an explanation of hitherto unexplained eye-tracking data, something none of the alternative accounts provide.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the inverse base-rate effect, a cognitive bias in category learning, and finds it persists even when supervised learning elements (prediction error signals) are removed through observational and unsupervised procedures. The authors propose a new theory called OSCAR that explains this bias using self-generated feedback akin to pattern completion, and demonstrate it outperforms alternatives by reproducing individual differences across all three learning procedures and explaining eye-tracking data.
AI.motivation: Existing prominent theories explain the inverse base-rate effect through prediction error in predictive-learning designs. This paper challenges this view by testing whether the effect persists when the error signals that supply prediction error are progressively removed, and whether current computational models can explain the bias in such contexts.
AI.method: Two experiments progressively removed prediction-error elements: (1) moved from predictive to observational learning, (2) moved to an unsupervised procedure without category labels. The authors then proposed OSCAR, a new theory integrating core computational principles of best-validated models, which operates on self-generated feedback akin to pattern completion. The model was evaluated on a large preexisting supervised dataset plus the two new experiments.
AI.result: The inverse base-rate effect persisted in both new procedures, indicating the bias is independent of supervised learning. OSCAR performed competitively against alternatives and was the first model to reproduce individual differences across all three procedures. It also uniquely explained previously unexplained eye-tracking data, which alternative accounts could not.
AI.conclusion: The inverse base-rate effect is not dependent on supervised learning or prediction error signals. OSCAR provides a unified computational account of the bias across predictive, observational, and unsupervised procedures by leveraging self-generated feedback through pattern completion, and offers superior explanatory power including previously unexplained eye-tracking phenomena.

title: PyOMES: an open-source framework for biochemical process modelling
summary: PyOMES is a Python-based, Open-source Modelling Environment for (bio)chemical process Simulation that aims to simplify the modelling of dynamic (including steady state) processes. This is done in a generalied, modular way to facilitate modelling a broad range of biological, chemical, and biochemical systems under a single modelling framework. PyOMES has been built to be accessible to a broad range of users - ranging from those with little modelling experience, such as experimentalists and students, through to more experienced power-users. Here, an introduction is provided to the PyOMES software including a summary of the design, architecture and vision. Use cases are then provided to demonstrate applicability of PyOMES to a number of (bio)chemical process modelling scenarios. Comparisons of predictions against existing benchmark software (i.e. PHREEQC) demonstrate the robustness of the package. Finally, a summary is provided of future directions for the PyOMES package - highlighting its establishment as a unified modelling framework and its potential for community-driven improvement as future developments.

AI.tldr: PyOMES is an open-source Python modelling environment for dynamic and steady-state (bio)chemical process simulation, designed to be modular and accessible to a broad range of users. It is validated against benchmark software like PHREEQC, demonstrating robustness, and aims to serve as a unified community-driven modelling framework.
AI.motivation: To simplify the modelling of dynamic (bio)chemical processes in a generalized, modular way that can handle a broad range of biological, chemical, and biochemical systems under a single framework, while being accessible to users with varying levels of modelling experience.
AI.method: PyOMES is designed as a Python-based, open-source modelling environment with a modular architecture. The paper provides a summary of its design, architecture, and vision, followed by use cases demonstrating applicability across various (bio)chemical process modelling scenarios.
AI.result: Predictions from PyOMES were compared against existing benchmark software (PHREEQC), demonstrating the robustness of the package across multiple (bio)chemical process modelling scenarios.
AI.conclusion: PyOMES is positioned as a unified modelling framework with potential for community-driven improvement, with future developments aimed at expanding its applicability and capabilities.

title: MS-MLB: An Open Machine Learning Benchmark for Blood-Based MS Classification
summary: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is diagnosed through clinical assessment, magnetic resonance imaging, laboratory evidence when appropriate, and exclusion of better explanations. Blood RNA expression data may contain disease associated immune signal, but a blood RNA classifier cannot be treated as a replacement for clinical diagnosis. This paper presents MS-MLB (Multiple Sclerosis Machine Learning Benchmark), a reproducible open benchmark for machine learning based MS research classification from whole blood RNA expression data. MS-MLB uses the public GSE17048 cohort, converts it into an MS versus healthy control task, and evaluates multiple algorithms under a shared, leakage controlled pipeline that a researcher can rerun without reconfiguring the evaluation. The evaluation includes nested cross-validation, an untouched stratified holdout set, bootstrap confidence intervals, ROC and precision recall analysis, calibration measurement, and an exploratory MS Research Score. In the final benchmark summary, Gradient Boosting ranked first by MS Research Score on the holdout set, with an MS Research Score of 93.83, AUC-ROC of 0.989, sensitivity of 0.950, specificity of 0.778, $F_{1}$ score of 0.927, and Brier score of 0.050. Prior studies have applied machine learning to MS blood transcriptomic data, including PBMC stage classification and whole blood diagnostic signature modeling. The contribution here is different and narrower. To our knowledge, MS-MLB is the first open benchmark focused on MS versus healthy control classification from GSE17048 whole blood RNA expression data with a documented external model submission pathway built into the framework. The score is intended for research comparison only and has not been clinically validated. The benchmark is accessible here: https://github.com/duckyquang/MS-MLB.

AI.tldr: MS-MLB is a reproducible open benchmark for machine learning classification of multiple sclerosis vs. healthy controls from whole blood RNA expression data (GSE17048), featuring a leakage-controlled pipeline, nested cross-validation, holdout testing, and an exploratory MS Research Score. Gradient Boosting achieved the top MS Research Score of 93.83 with AUC-ROC of 0.989 on the holdout set.
AI.motivation: Multiple sclerosis diagnosis is complex and relies on multiple modalities. Blood RNA expression data may carry disease-related immune signals, but there is a lack of standardized, reproducible benchmarks for evaluating ML classifiers on MS blood transcriptomic data, making it difficult to compare approaches fairly.
AI.method: The paper constructs MS-MLB using the public GSE17048 cohort, framing an MS vs. healthy control classification task. It evaluates multiple ML algorithms under a shared, leakage-controlled pipeline with nested cross-validation, an untouched stratified holdout set, bootstrap confidence intervals, ROC and precision-recall analysis, calibration measurement, and an MS Research Score. The framework includes a documented external model submission pathway.
AI.result: Gradient Boosting ranked first by MS Research Score (93.83) on the holdout set, with AUC-ROC of 0.989, sensitivity of 0.950, specificity of 0.778, F1 of 0.927, and Brier score of 0.050.
AI.conclusion: MS-MLB is the first open benchmark focused specifically on MS vs. healthy control classification from GSE17048 whole blood RNA data with a built-in external model submission pathway. The score is for research comparison only and has not been clinically validated.

title: Toward a Dynamical Taxonomy of Insomnia: A Multiaxial Framework for Sleep-State Transitions and Architectural Failure
summary: Insomnia disorder is defined at the syndrome level, yet similar complaints can arise from different abnormalities in sleep regulation, state transition, state stabilization, spatial recruitment, architectural sequencing, and state perception. We propose a multiaxial dynamical framework whose principal contribution is organizational: a candidate profile is specified by the dynamical operation that fails, the sleep stage or boundary at which it fails, and its causal status. Objective sleep duration, age, circadian phase, comorbidity, medication exposure, and night-to-night variability are modifier/covariate dimensions rather than additional mechanistic classes. A local Landau-Ginzburg formalism, adopted from prior cortical and sleep-dynamics work, supplies a phenomenological language for nested hypotheses. Its relaxational form applies only to boundary-local dynamics under an approximate gradient description; non-gradient escape requires an action or quasipotential treatment, and whole-night REM-NREM sequencing requires reactive or oscillatory dynamics. Routine polysomnography usually identifies effective combinations rather than curvature, escape action, bias, noise, and relaxation separately. The strongest boundary-level evidence concerns sleep onset, where published results are consistent with bifurcation-like or bistable dynamics but do not yet exclude a driven smooth transition produced by the homeostatic-circadian ramp. The remaining operation classes are hypothesis-generating extensions. The taxonomy is judged by pragmatic utility, including improved communication, stratification, and prediction; the scalar-field implementation and specific dynamical profiles are separately falsifiable. The framework is a phenomenological organizing model rather than a new diagnosis, validated biomarker, or treatment-selection system.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multiaxial dynamical framework for classifying insomnia disorder, organized by the dynamical operation that fails, the sleep stage or boundary where it fails, and its causal status, with objective sleep duration, age, circadian phase, comorbidity, medication, and night-to-night variability as modifying covariates rather than mechanistic classes.
AI.motivation: Insomnia is currently defined at the syndrome level, but similar complaints can arise from fundamentally different underlying abnormalities in sleep regulation, state transitions, stabilization, spatial recruitment, architectural sequencing, and state perception. A more precise, mechanism-oriented organizational framework is needed to improve communication, stratification, and prediction.
AI.method: A multiaxial dynamical framework is proposed, organized by (1) the dynamical operation that fails, (2) the sleep stage or boundary at which it fails, and (3) causal status. A local Landau-Ginzburg formalism provides a phenomenological language for nested hypotheses, distinguishing relaxational (gradient) dynamics for boundary-local processes, action/quasipotential treatments for non-gradient escape, and reactive/oscillatory dynamics for whole-night REM-NREM sequencing.
AI.result: Routine polysomnography typically identifies effective combinations rather than isolating curvature, escape action, bias, noise, and relaxation separately. The strongest boundary-level evidence is at sleep onset, where published results are consistent with bifurcation-like or bistable dynamics but do not exclude a driven smooth transition from a homeostatic-circadian ramp. Other operation classes remain hypothesis-generating extensions.
AI.conclusion: The taxonomy is judged by pragmatic utility for improved communication, stratification, and prediction. The framework is a phenomenological organizing model rather than a new diagnosis, validated biomarker, or treatment-selection system. The scalar-field implementation and specific dynamical profiles are separately falsifiable, and the primary contribution is organizational.

title: A Quantum Circuit Framework for Protein Ensemble-Level Energetics
comment: Please see github repo https://github.com/pra-ashok/QProtSim for code and supplementary information. A Pypi package qprotsim is also available at https://pypi.org/project/qprotsim/
summary: Proteins occupy heterogeneous free-energy landscapes in which high-entropy ensembles converge toward compact, low-energy basins with multiple sub-states. Molecular dynamics can access these landscapes at atomic resolution, but exhaustive sampling remains computationally demanding. Meanwhile, most quantum approaches target only single optimal structures, leaving full ensemble energetic heterogeneity unexplored. We introduce a residue-level, gate-based quantum circuit framework for coarse-graining protein thermodynamics. Each amino acid is represented as a two-state qubit (stabilised vs. excited solvation state) based on residue solvation energetics. A structure-informed entanglement block then encodes covalent and non-covalent contacts using parameterised controlled gates, embedding correlations across the residue-interaction network. Sampling the circuit ($\sim 10^6$ measurements) yields binary thermodynamic microstates used to compute protein energy distributions, residue-level statistical couplings, energetic sensitivities, and information gains relative to total free energy. We showcase the framework on the benchmark Trp-cage miniprotein 1L2Y (TC5b) and 9GDL, a disulfide-stabilised Trp-cage-fortified exenatide chimera. For 1L2Y, the circuit reproduces a structured, folding-funnel-like energy distribution. Comparative analysis with 9GDL reveals shifts in global energy distributions and residue-level stability profiles. Coupling and information-theoretic analyses localise residues associated with ensemble reorganisation, while multi-body couplings show the circuit resolves both direct and indirect statistical correlations. This framework expands quantum protein modelling beyond single-structure optimisation toward ensemble-level characterisation, capturing key features of rugged energy landscapes to guide protein design, mutation mapping, and allosteric pathway identification.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a residue-level, gate-based quantum circuit framework for coarse-graining protein thermodynamics, representing each amino acid as a two-state qubit and using structure-informed entanglement to sample binary thermodynamic microstates that capture energy distributions, statistical couplings, and information gains. Validated on Trp-cage miniprotein 1L2Y and its chimera 9GDL, the framework reproduces folding-funnel-like energy landscapes and localizes ensemble-reorganization residues, extending quantum protein modeling to ensemble-level characterization beyond single-structure optimization.
AI.motivation: Proteins occupy heterogeneous free-energy landscapes with multiple sub-states that are computationally expensive to sample exhaustively via molecular dynamics at atomic resolution. Meanwhile, most quantum approaches target only single optimal structures, leaving the full ensemble energetic heterogeneity unexplored. There is a need for a method that captures ensemble-level thermodynamics efficiently.
AI.method: Each amino acid is mapped to a two-state qubit (stabilised vs. excited solvation state) based on residue solvation energetics. A structure-informed entanglement block encodes covalent and non-covalent contacts using parameterised controlled gates, embedding correlations across the residue-interaction network. Circuit sampling (~10^6 measurements) yields binary thermodynamic microstates used to compute protein energy distributions, residue-level statistical couplings, energetic sensitivities, and information gains.
AI.result: For 1L2Y, the circuit reproduces a structured, folding-funnel-like energy distribution. Comparative analysis with 9GDL reveals shifts in global energy distributions and residue-level stability profiles. Coupling and information-theoretic analyses localise residues associated with ensemble reorganisation, and multi-body couplings confirm the circuit resolves both direct and indirect statistical correlations.
AI.conclusion: This framework expands quantum protein modelling beyond single-structure optimisation toward ensemble-level characterisation, capturing key features of rugged energy landscapes to guide protein design, mutation mapping, and allosteric pathway identification.

title: Two base rates, two weights: base-rate neglect has a second axis
comment: 33 pages, 14 figures. Code to reproduce all formal claims and figures: https://osf.io/9qvbr/
summary: Base-rate neglect is usually treated as one mistake: giving the prior too little weight. Turning the co-occurrences you see into a useful judgment, though, means correcting for two base rates, not one. The first is the familiar prior, how common the outcome is. The second is how common the cue itself is. Those are two separate mistakes, and a learner can make either one alone. Under-correcting the prior is classical base-rate neglect; under-correcting the cue is the cue-density effect of contingency learning, long studied but not previously recognised as a kind of base-rate neglect. We write both corrections as two weights in one Bayesian equation. The task decides which weight it can measure: the cue-frequency weight appears only in graded ratings, because a two-choice test cancels it. At their extremes the two weights recover familiar quantities: base-rate neglect, the signal-detection criterion, the contiguity/sensitivity/validity triple, and the "lift" measure of causal strength. The same cue-frequency weight also sits inside six standard learning-and-memory models; they seem to agree, but only because the usual experiments squeeze the data into a form where they cannot disagree. Above all, the two neglects should be separately manipulable: an experimenter can move one without moving the other. That is a double dissociation, and a one-parameter account cannot produce it. That prediction is the framework's centre, and it has not yet been tested. This paper lays out the framework and the rating experiment that would settle it; a companion paper fits the two weights to an existing colour-flavour dataset.

AI.tldr: This paper reframes base-rate neglect as two distinct errors—under-weighting the outcome's prior and under-weighting the cue's frequency—unified in a single Bayesian equation. The cue-frequency weight is measurable only in graded ratings (canceled in two-choice tests), recovers familiar quantities (base-rate neglect, signal-detection criterion, sensitivity, lift), and appears inside six learning models. The central untested prediction is a double dissociation between the two neglects, which a one-parameter account cannot produce.
AI.motivation: Base-rate neglect has been treated as a single mistake (giving the prior too little weight), but the authors argue that correct judgment from co-occurrences requires correcting for two base rates: outcome frequency and cue frequency. They aim to unify classical base-rate neglect with the cue-density effect from contingency learning, showing these are two separable errors governed by separate weights.
AI.method: The authors formulate both corrections as two weights in a single Bayesian equation. They analyze how task design determines which weight is measurable—two-choice tests cancel the cue-frequency weight while graded ratings reveal it. They show extremes of the weights recover known measures (base-rate neglect, signal-detection criterion, contiguity/sensitivity/validity, lift) and demonstrate the cue-frequency weight is embedded in six standard learning-and-memory models. They propose a rating experiment to test the framework's central prediction of double dissociation between the two neglects.
AI.result: The framework shows the two neglects are separately manipulable and constitute a double dissociation that no one-parameter account can produce. The prediction remains untested; a companion paper fits the two weights to an existing color-flavour dataset. The authors argue standard experiments cannot distinguish the models because data are squeezed into forms that preclude disagreement.
AI.conclusion: Base-rate neglect should be reconceived as two independent errors—prior neglect and cue-density neglect—with separate weights in one Bayesian framework. The central prediction of double dissociation needs empirical testing via graded-rating experiments, which the paper lays out as the key next step.

title: Multiparametric MRI Radiomics and Machine Learning Framework for Predicting Treatment Response in Glioblastoma
summary: Distinguishing True Progression (TP) from Pseudo-Progression (PsP) after chemoradiotherapy remains a major diagnostic challenge in GBM, as both entities present near-identical appearances on conventional contrast-enhanced post-treatment MRI. This distinction carries substantial clinical weight, since TP and PsP demand divergent management yet cannot be reliably separated on routine imaging alone. We investigated whether radiomic features derived from a parsimonious, voxel-wise pharmacokinetic model of dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI, combined with MGMT status, could discriminate between the two. The cohort comprised 82 adults with IDH-wildtype GBM who developed a new contrast-enhancing lesion within six months of chemoradiotherapy; classification (53 TP, 29 PsP) was established by histopathology where available (n=52) and modified RANO criteria otherwise (n=30). At every voxel, contrast-concentration time courses were fitted to five candidate pharmacokinetic models, and the best fit was retained by AIC minimisation, yielding parsimonious Ktrans, Ve, Vp, and taui maps adapting to local heterogeneity rather than a single fixed model across the tumour. Following segmentation, 1,073 radiomic descriptors were extracted and reduced via Mann-Whitney U filtering and Elastic Net, then used to train five classifiers across four feature configurations. A Random Forest classifier combining parsimonious DCE-MRI radiomics with MGMT status achieved the best discrimination (mean AUC 0.89, sensitivity 0.93, specificity 0.76, F1 0.90), outperforming features without MGMT (0.84), a T1-post-contrast baseline (0.72), and a single-model extended-Tofts analysis (0.68). Shape and textural descriptors of the Ktrans map, with tumour volume, were the strongest predictors, MGMT contributing a smaller, independent effect. Allowing the model to vary voxel-wise improves non-invasive discrimination.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether radiomic features from a parsimonious voxel-wise pharmacokinetic model of DCE-MRI, combined with MGMT status, can distinguish true progression (TP) from pseudo-progression (PsP) in GBM patients after chemoradiotherapy. Using 82 patients, a Random Forest classifier with parsimonious DCE-MRI radiomics plus MGMT status achieved the best discrimination (AUC 0.89), outperforming baseline and single-model approaches.
AI.motivation: Distinguishing true progression from pseudo-progression after chemoradiotherapy in GBM is a major clinical challenge, as both appear nearly identical on conventional MRI but require divergent management. Routine imaging alone cannot reliably separate these entities, motivating the need for improved non-invasive discrimination methods.
AI.method: 82 adults with IDH-wildtype GBM and new contrast-enhancing lesions within 6 months of chemoradiotherapy were analyzed (53 TP, 29 PsP). DCE-MRI contrast-concentration time courses were fitted to five candidate pharmacokinetic models per voxel, with best fit retained by AIC minimization to generate parsimonious Ktrans, Ve, Vp, and taui maps. 1,073 radiomic descriptors were extracted, reduced via Mann-Whitney U filtering and Elastic Net, and used to train five classifiers across four feature configurations.
AI.result: A Random Forest classifier combining parsimonious DCE-MRI radiomics with MGMT status achieved the best discrimination (mean AUC 0.89, sensitivity 0.93, specificity 0.76, F1 0.90), outperforming features without MGMT (0.84), T1-post-contrast baseline (0.72), and single-model extended-Tofts analysis (0.68). Shape and textural features of the Ktrans map plus tumor volume were strongest predictors, with MGMT contributing a smaller independent effect.
AI.conclusion: Allowing the pharmacokinetic model to vary voxel-wise improves non-invasive discrimination between TP and PsP in GBM, demonstrating that parsimonious DCE-MRI radiomics combined with MGMT status provides a clinically valuable approach where conventional imaging falls short.

title: THBKG: A Temporal Biomedical Knowledge Graph for Decision-Aligned Clinical Advancement Prediction
summary: Inadequate target--disease linkage accounts for 40--50\% of Phase~II efficacy failures, so anticipating which programmes will advance would let sponsors back the hypotheses most likely to reach patients. What a programme can be judged on is the evidence that supported its linkage \emph{when it entered the clinic}. No existing biomedical knowledge graph allows that evidence profile to be assembled as of a past date. We present the Temporal Heterogeneous Biomedical Knowledge Graph (THBKG), which describes and predicts therapeutic target--disease links through time: 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across nineteen relation types, each edge carrying the year its evidence changed, so a pair's profile can be recovered as it stood when its own decision fell due. On this graph we define a decision-aligned benchmark that predicts, for a target--disease pair entering Phase~II, whether it advances to Phase~III on evidence datable before that decision. Graph propagation over the THBKG outranks every direct-evidence reference scored under the same decision-aligned protocol, reaching a relative success of 4.3--4.5 at the top ten pairs per therapeutic area. The gain concentrates on the 72.8\% of pairs with no direct target--disease evidence at their decision point, where a direct-edge model has nothing to read: the encoders still rank five- to sixfold above chance, recovering the signal by propagating over the intervening biology. Adapting a path-based explainer to the decision-time subgraph decomposes each prediction into the evidence landscape behind the hypothesis for explainable prediction. We release the THBKG as a continually updated substrate for studying therapeutic target hypotheses by retrospective validation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces THBKG, a temporal heterogeneous biomedical knowledge graph with 110,396 entities and 11.1M time-stamped edges, designed to reconstruct target-disease evidence profiles as they existed at any past decision point. A decision-aligned benchmark predicts Phase II-to-III advancement, where graph propagation outperforms direct-evidence models, especially for the 72.8% of pairs lacking direct evidence, achieving 4.3-4.5x relative success.
AI.motivation: 40-50% of Phase II efficacy failures stem from inadequate target-disease linkage. Sponsors need to predict which programs will advance, but no existing knowledge graph can reconstruct the evidence profile of a target-disease pair as it stood when the program entered the clinic—a critical historical perspective for retrospective validation.
AI.method: Construct THBKG with 110,396 entities, 11.1M edges across 19 relation types, where each edge carries the year its evidence changed, allowing temporal reconstruction of evidence profiles. Define a decision-aligned benchmark predicting Phase II-to-III advancement based only on evidence datable before the decision. Use graph propagation over the THBKG and adapt a path-based explainer to the decision-time subgraph.
AI.result: Graph propagation over THBKG outperforms all direct-evidence reference models under the decision-aligned protocol, achieving 4.3-4.5x relative success at top ten pairs per therapeutic area. For the 72.8% of pairs with no direct evidence, encoders still rank 5-6x above chance by propagating over intervening biology.
AI.conclusion: Temporal knowledge graphs with evidence-dated edges enable decision-aligned retrospective validation of therapeutic target hypotheses. The THBKG is released as a continually updated substrate for studying target-disease links, with explainable predictions decomposing each decision into its underlying evidence landscape.

title: EpiBench: Can LLMs Understand Epitopes for Antibody Drug Discovery?
summary: Epitopes determine where antibodies bind antigens and shape downstream therapeutic properties such as functional blockade and escape resistance, making epitope understanding central to antibody drug discovery. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong biomedical reasoning ability, it remains unclear whether they can infer epitope information directly from antigen and antibody sequences. Existing epitope resources typically focus on isolated prediction tasks or rely on specialized structural settings, while general protein benchmarks do not evaluate epitope-centered decisions across the antibody development workflow. To address this gap, we introduce EpiBench, a closed-book, sequence-based, and automatically scorable benchmark for evaluating epitope reasoning in LLMs. EpiBench contains 1,609 curated samples grounded in structural antibody--antigen contacts, curated functional B-cell assays, and deep mutational scanning escape measurements. It covers five connected tasks: targetable region discovery, antibody-conditioned epitope identification, epitope binning, functional epitope assessment, and antibody escape assessment, with controlled sampling to reduce shortcut-based evaluation artifacts. We evaluate nine general-purpose LLMs and analyze their behavior through task-specific baselines, antigen length stratification, explicit-reasoning comparison, and failure-mode inspection. The results show that current LLMs capture partial epitope-related signals but remain limited in antibody-specific sequence grounding, long-context residue localization, and biologically grounded reasoning. Therefore, EpiBench provides a diagnostic testbed for measuring and improving sequence-aware biomedical LLMs toward reliable LLM-assisted antibody discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EpiBench, a closed-book, sequence-based, automatically scorable benchmark for evaluating epitope reasoning in large language models. It contains 1,609 curated samples spanning five connected tasks (targetable region discovery, antibody-conditioned epitope identification, epitope binning, functional epitope assessment, and antibody escape assessment). Evaluation of nine LLMs shows they capture partial epitope-related signals but remain limited in antibody-specific sequence grounding, long-context residue localization, and biologically grounded reasoning.
AI.motivation: Epitope understanding is central to antibody drug discovery, yet it remains unclear whether LLMs can infer epitope information directly from antigen and antibody sequences. Existing epitope resources focus on isolated prediction tasks or specialized structural settings, while general protein benchmarks do not evaluate epitope-centered decisions across the antibody development workflow.
AI.method: EpiBench provides a benchmark with 1,609 curated samples grounded in structural antibody-antigen contacts, curated functional B-cell assays, and deep mutational scanning escape measurements. It covers five connected tasks with controlled sampling to reduce shortcut-based evaluation artifacts. Nine general-purpose LLMs are evaluated using task-specific baselines, antigen length stratification, explicit-reasoning comparison, and failure-mode inspection.
AI.result: Current LLMs capture partial epitope-related signals but remain limited in three key areas: antibody-specific sequence grounding, long-context residue localization, and biologically grounded reasoning.
AI.conclusion: EpiBench serves as a diagnostic testbed for measuring and improving sequence-aware biomedical LLMs toward reliable LLM-assisted antibody discovery.
